finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the whole request body onto the authenticated user object and saves it. An attacker can set privileged fields such as role, isAdmin, id, email-verified or tenant, which escalates privileges or changes ownership.
finding.source: req.body, the JSON body of PUT /me, which any authenticated user controls
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user), which persists the attacker-chosen fields

trace.note: PUT /me handler reads the request body
Object.assign merges all body keys into req.user with no field allowlist
The user is returned in the response

finding.guards_checked: The handler has no field allowlist, schema validation or role check. The sibling route /me/profile destructures only displayName and bio, which shows the intended safe pattern and that this route lacks it. I could not see any middleware outside this file, since only users.js exists. Object.assign does not trigger the __proto__ setter for an own JSON key, so prototype pollution is not the issue here.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist, schema or role check, then users.js:6 saves and users.js:7 returns it, so any authenticated user can set privileged fields; the sibling route at users.js:11 destructures only displayName and bio, and users.js is the only file so no outside middleware or model-level field protection is visible.
